children: New Delhi, Sept. 23 -- Industrialist Venu Srinivasan is trending this week after publicly defying a directive from the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) that tried to stop him from voting on Tata Sons' proposed IPO. He voted for the listing anyway, calling the Trust's move invalid, a stand that has renewed attention on one of India's more understated figures. Here's a closer look at who he is.

Srinivasan, a non-executive director on the Tata Sons board, was one of four directors who voted in favour of reappointing N Chandrasekaran as chairman of Tata Sons and the proposed listing of the Tata group holding company at a board meeting held this week, with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata casting the sole dissenting vote.

The vote followed a resolution by SDTT, a major Tata Sons shareholder, seeking to bar Srinivasan from voting after he took a public position at odds with the Trust's preference to keep Tata Sons private.

Srinivasan pushed back in writing, stating the directive was issued without consultation and conflicted with his legal duty as a director to act in the interests of Tata Sons as a whole, not any single shareholder.

Venu Srinivasan is the grandson of T V Sundaram Iyengar, who founded the TVS Group in 1911. He studied engineering at the College of Engineering, Guindy, part of Anna University, before completing a management degree at Purdue University in the United States.

Srinivasan took over as managing director of what was then Sundaram-Clayton's two-wheeler business in the early 1980s and is widely credited with steering TVS Motor Company's growth into one of India's largest two- and three-wheeler manufacturers, with factories across India and units in Indonesia and the United Kingdom.

Under his stewardship, the company's brakes division won Japan's Deming Prize in 1998 for quality management, and he personally received the Ishikawa-Kano Award in 2012 for his contribution to quality practices at TVS.
He stepped back from day-to-day leadership in August last year, when his son, Sudarshan Venu, took over as chairman and managing director of TVS Motor.
Srinivasan now holds the title of Chairman Emeritus of TVS Motor and non-executive chairman of TVS Holdings.
Beyond TVS, Srinivasan has served on the Tata Sons board since 2016 and is Vice-Chairman of the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), one of the two largest charitable trusts that control Tata Sons.
He was reappointed as a life trustee of SDTT last October, just before his three-year term was due to end, cementing his standing within the Trusts.
He previously raised objections at a meeting last November to the way the Trusts have handled internal governance matters, including the process used to induct new trustees.

Srinivasan's decision to vote against a Trust directive marks a rare and public instance of a Tata Sons director asserting independence from the Trusts that control the group, and comes as the Reserve Bank of India continues to push large non-banking finance companies toward public listing.
Neither Tata Sons nor Tata Trusts has issued a detailed statement beyond the positions taken by Srinivasan and Noel Tata at the board meeting.
Srinivasan was appointed a non-official director on the Reserve Bank of India's Central Board in 2022. He was awarded the Padma Bhushan, India's third-highest civilian honour, in 2020.

He also holds honorary ties with South Korea, having served as Honorary Consul General of the Republic of Korea in Chennai and received that country's Order of Diplomatic Service Merit in 2010 for his role in strengthening India-Korea business relations.
Separately, he chairs the Board of Trustees of the Srirangam Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple. Forbes has listed him among the world's billionaires in its 2026 rankings.
